node.label: Laura F. Edwards
node.date_label: Gendered Strife and Confusion (1997) · Scarlett Doesn’t Live Here Anymore (2000) · The People and Their Peace (2009) · A Legal History of the Civil War and Reconstruction (2015) · Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022)
node.description: In The People and Their Peace (2009), Laura F. Edwards argues that local legal practice gave people without individual rights a place in maintaining the social order of the post-Revolutionary Carolinas. Centralization around individual rights could therefore reproduce and intensify racial, gender and class inequalities by excluding people who had previously participated through their subordinate status. Gendered Strife and Confusion (1997) connects household gender relations to Reconstruction politics; Scarlett Doesn’t Live Here Anymore (2000) brings Black and yeoman women into a broader synthesis of southern women’s history. Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022) follows textiles as property and economic resources that people with limited rights could possess and exchange. The People and Their Peace won the Littleton-Griswold and Charles Sydnor prizes, but its interpretation remains contested. Tim Huebner praised its recovery of localized law while challenging its treatment of state appellate courts and their protection of enslaved people’s procedural rights. Jessica K. Lowe questioned the sharp division between local and state law and the account of localized law’s popular content.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Gendered Strife and Confusion: The Political Culture of Reconstruction (1997); Scarlett Doesn’t Live Here Anymore: Southern Women in the Civil War Era (2000; paperback 2004); The People and Their Peace: Legal Culture and the Transformation of Inequality in the Post-Revolutionary South (2009); A Legal History of the Civil War and Reconstruction: A Nation of Rights (2015); Only the Clothes on Her Back: Clothing and the Hidden History of Power in the Nineteenth-Century United States (2022).
node.scope_note: The 2022 book was read in a licensed preview: title/copyright, acknowledgments pp. ix–xiii and selected introduction pp. 1–9. Complete Huebner and Frisby reviews and the AHA interview were read. The 1997 and 2009 books are represented by publisher descriptions and named reviewers; Lowe’s essay by its abstract only. Complete monographs, most listed articles, and the particular Faust and Fox-Genovese works synthesized in Scarlett remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022), Edwards credits Jacquelyn Dowd Hall with sustained guidance of the manuscript through their writing group and with inspiring her historical writing.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Acknowledgments pp. xii–xiii, licensed preview: Hall’s group “read and reread” the project from proposals to manuscript; the following paragraph singles out Hall as a model for writing history. These are explicit scholarly and manuscript debts. No doctoral-supervision claim is inferred; remaining book chapters unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2022 AHA interview, Edwards identifies E. P. Thompson’s Whigs and Hunters (1975) as a favorite book that she repeatedly reads.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: AHA interview, question asking for a recommended book: “One of my favorite books” names Whigs and Hunters and refers to rereading it. This is deliberately limited to her stated reading and admiration, not agreement with any particular thesis or proof of direct derivation. Original year checked in Peluso’s review, p. 309; Thompson’s book itself unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Scarlett Doesn’t Live Here Anymore (2000), Edwards brings Black and yeoman women into the center of southern women’s history while synthesizing research for a wider readership.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Frisby review, opening statement of the book’s aim (quoting p. 2) and final substantive paragraph. Frisby praises this recovery while also criticizing gaps in domestic and family life beyond labor and law. Book read through this named reviewer only.
proposed_edges.map_label: Black and yeoman women at the center

proposed_edges.relationship: Gendered Strife and Confusion (1997) explains how ideas about women’s and men’s household roles shaped political conflict during Reconstruction across racial and class divisions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Illinois Press, About the Book, both paragraphs: links household roles with groups’ understandings of public politics and extends the process beyond 1877. A substantive named framework, not a link based on the author’s faculty field classification. Publisher description only; full book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022) connects textiles’ material qualities and legal standing to their use as property and economic resources by people with weak claims to rights.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 1–3 and 6–9 in the licensed preview: possession, exchange and material evidence connect textiles to economic participation. Scope is the book’s explicit intervention in material-culture history; it is not a claim of unrestricted property rights. Rest of book unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Textiles as legally protected material resources

proposed_edges.relationship: Edwards’s essay on marriage, households and the politics of Reconstruction in North Carolina appeared in Jumpin’ Jim Crow (2000), the collection Glenda Elizabeth Gilmore co-edited with Jane Dailey and Bryant Simon.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Two permitted witnesses. (1) Edwards’s 2023 Princeton vita, p. 3–4, under her 1996 Law and History Review article: “republished as ‘Marriage, Households, and the Politics of Reconstruction in North Carolina,’ in Glenda Gilmore, Jane Dailey, and Bryant Simon, eds., Race, Gender, and Politics in the New South, 1865-1980 (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2000), 7-27”. (2) Yale Black Studies page for Jumpin’ Jim Crow (Princeton, 2000): editors “Jane Dailey, Glenda Elizabeth Gilmore, Bryant Simon”; “In addition to the editors, the contributors are … Laura F. Edwards …”. The vita’s title is evidently a working title: same press, year and three editors, and Edwards is listed among Jumpin’ Jim Crow’s contributors. This is an editor–contributor link, the kind the coordinator accepted for dgw_w_03 (White’s Telling Histories). It is thin: one of twelve contributors besides the three editors, and no text says Gilmore shaped Edwards’s argument. Flag to the outside reviewers. Hall is also among the contributors, which gives Hall nothing new (Gilmore is already her partner).
proposed_edges.map_label: Essay in Gilmore’s co-edited Jumpin’ Jim Crow

proposed_edges.relationship: Edwards published “At the Threshold of the Plantation Household: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese and Southern Women’s History” (Mississippi Quarterly, 2012), an essay on Fox-Genovese’s place in southern women’s history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Title-level evidence only. Princeton University research portal record: title, author Laura F. Edwards, Mississippi Quarterly 65:4 (September 2012), pp. 577–589, DOI 10.1353/mss.2012.0008; no abstract and no attached file. The article body (Project MUSE) returned a verification challenge to both the web tool and a plain request; it was not pursued, so the essay is unread. The relationship sentence says only what the title states: a whole essay whose subject is Fox-Genovese and southern women’s history. No argument, praise or critique is attributed. Hence comparison, undirected, and no critique typing. This is not the held lfe_w_05, which rested on a reviewer’s list in Frisby’s review of Scarlett. Verifier: hold if title-level evidence is below the bar; restore with fuller wording if the MUSE text can be read from another network.
proposed_edges.map_label: Essay on Fox-Genovese and southern women’s history

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Dylan Penningroth's Before the Movement in 2024, Eric Foner writes that Penningroth's work builds on that of Laura Edwards and Martha S. Jones, who have expanded legal history to include the role of law in everyday life and argued that law is made also by people with limited representation in legislatures and courts.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on the magazine’s own site. The paragraph beginning Penningroth insists that the standard narrative explicitly names Edwards and Martha S. Jones, then describes their argument about ordinary people creating law despite limited representation. This is substantive engagement with a specified argument, rather than a list of scholars sharing a topic. The relationship records Foner’s assessment, not an independently established debt on Penningroth’s part; no separate edge to Penningroth is proposed. Foner does not identify a particular Edwards book in this paragraph. Elsewhere in the review he dates Roll, Jordan, Roll to 1974, supporting the original year used in bf3_02.
proposed_edges.map_label: Foner places Edwards's everyday legal history

proposed_edges.relationship: In The People and Their Peace (2009), Edwards discusses the argument in Eugene Genovese’s Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974) that exceptions favoring individual enslaved people affirmed the underlying logic of the system.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Limited primary-text evidence: read the Google Books search-within-volume excerpt for Genovese, result PA251 (printed p. 251), not the full page or chapter. The excerpt expressly attributes an argument to Genovese’s named book in body text. It continues into a qualification beginning But that logic and then cuts off; therefore this edge asserts discussion of the stated argument only, not Edwards’s agreement, intellectual debt, or the scope of her criticism. The full-page preview reported a viewing limit, which was respected. This is not a footnote citation or an acknowledgment. Publication of Edwards’s book in 2009 was separately checked on the UNC Press page; Foner’s 2024 review confirms Genovese’s original 1974 date. The restricted reading scope must remain attached to this edge at review.

proposed_edges.relationship: Laura F. Edwards's Gendered Strife and Confusion (1997) contributes to the political history of Reconstruction by explaining how household gender roles shaped elite and poor, Black and white southerners' understandings of public life and their places in it.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's complete two-paragraph description and publication metadata. The following sentence explains how household roles shaped different groups' views of the public arena; the second paragraph describes Reconstruction as conflict and negotiation extending beyond 1877. This is a bounded field contribution supported by a publisher synopsis, not evidence of a later scholar's adoption. The book itself was not read. Endorsements are not used. The political endpoint is distinct from the existing gender endpoint, although the contributions overlap.

proposed_edges.relationship: Laura F. Edwards's Only the Clothes on Her Back (2022) contributes to economic history by reconstructing how legal practices made textiles property that marginalized people could use as currency, credit and capital in the early United States.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete four-paragraph publisher abstract and publication metadata. It explicitly connects textiles' legally protected value to participation in the economy and describes the book's revision of production and exchange. The field mapping concerns property and economic transactions, extending beyond the existing consumption/material-culture pair. Abstract only: the book's chapters remain unread, and no particular scholar's debt is inferred.
proposed_edges.map_label: Textiles as currency, credit and capital
